topic.title: We'd laugh at this CV, but not at this marriage wishlist
topic.claim: If someone asked for a dream job with zero preparation we'd call it delusional, but we nod along when the same entitlement is applied to marriage.
topic.behaviour: A satirical post imagines a 30-year-old with no resume, no idea of deliverables and a wishlist of high pay, great work-life balance and a boss who understands he's new. It ends by saying that sounds ridiculous for a career but oddly normal in marriage posts.
topic.mechanism: We treat careers as something you earn through skills, but treat marriage as something that should simply fall into place for the right match. That leaves many people never examining what they bring to the table or what they're actually asking of another person.
topic.group: singles in their late 20s and 30s using arranged marriage
real_details: Satirical poster is 30M and says the 20s went on relationships
Has never written a resume and doesn't know what a deliverable is
Wants a high-paying job, work-life balance and supportive colleagues
Hopes everything will 'naturally fall into place' with the right company
Closing note compares it to how people talk about marriage and relationships on the sub
topic.why_now: The post is from this month's top threads and the sarcasm clearly landed.

score.why: Bold, plain analogy that hits a double standard everyone's lived near, in the 'eldest child' bluntness he likes.

paragraphs: Imagine a 30-year-old asking for a high-paying job with no resume. You'd laugh. Now put that same ask on a biodata. Why does nobody laugh?
Here's the candidate. He spent his 20s on relationships. Never written a resume. Doesn't know what a deliverable is.
He wants good pay, work-life balance and colleagues who get that he's new.
His plan? The right company will come along and everything will naturally fall into place.
Any HR person would close that tab in four seconds. Papa would give him a full lecture on ambition.
Now read a typical matrimony profile. Looking for someone caring, ambitious, family-oriented, financially stable.
What does he bring? "Simple guy, easy going."
It's the same candidate with the same plan, and everyone nods.
We all know a job doesn't just happen to you. You build skills, you sit through a bad first boss.
Marriage gets talked about like luck. Find the right match, done.
The funny part is that families do run a background check. Salary, company, does he own a flat.
They just run it on the other person.
Can you cook dinner on a weekday? Sit through a money fight without calling your mother?

draft.caption: What's one line you've seen on a biodata that would never survive a job interview?
draft.alt_text: A seven-slide text carousel comparing a 30-year-old who wants a high-paying job with no resume and no idea what a deliverable is to the way people approach arranged marriage. It argues that careers are treated as earned while marriage is treated as luck, that families check the other side's salary and flat but never their own child's readiness, and ends by asking whether you can cook a weekday dinner or handle a money fight, calling that the real resume.

hook_candidates.hook: Imagine a 30-year-old asking for a high-paying job with no resume. You'd laugh. Now put that same ask on a biodata. Why does nobody laugh?
Most Indian men on matrimony sites are asking for a job they'd never get hired for. And I know how that sounds.
We'd laugh at a guy asking for a dream job with no resume. Put the same ask on a biodata and everyone nods.
Dear 'simple guy, easy going' on every matrimony site, we need to talk about your resume.
No company would hire a guy with no resume and no skills. So why do families say yes to him on a biodata?
